title: Atomic operations, application races, and publication
summary: Choose synchronization from the invariant: one atomic operation is not a transaction over your whole algorithm.
objectives: Distinguish a data race from a race in application logic
Use compare-exchange to preserve a single-counter reservation invariant
Explain Relaxed versus Release/Acquire and the limits of SeqCst
Prevent deadlock through ownership and a consistent lock order
body:
Purpose: reserve work without inventing capacity

An indexer has room for one more job. Two workers each inspect the remaining capacity, decide there is room, and reserve it. Every memory access can be legal Rust while the application admits two jobs into one slot. This lesson separates memory safety from the business invariant, then asks what synchronization actually protects that invariant. Do not replace the indexer's channels with atomic counters merely because atomics sound faster. Its bounded channel already combines admission, waiting and ownership transfer. The focused lab makes the smaller decision visible.

Plain-English model: indivisible does not mean everything happens together

An atomic operation on a supported atomic type appears indivisible to other accesses to that same atomic object. Another thread does not observe half of one atomic integer store. A data race is a particular conflict involving concurrent memory accesses to the same location, at least one write and at least one non-atomic access, without the required synchronization; it is undefined behavior. Safe Rust's ownership rules and safe synchronization interfaces prevent data races within their sound contracts. A race condition in application logic is broader: a result depends on an ordering that violates your intended contract. Atomics can eliminate a data race while leaving a check-then-act race.

Our invariant is: successful reservations consume exactly their requested units, and the available count never goes below zero. A separate load, arithmetic operation and store do not form one atomic reservation. Picture two people copying the same ticket count before either changes it. The analogy explains the check-then-act conflict, but it says nothing about processor caches, compiler transformations or Rust's memory model. We will use the documented ordering rules for those.

Prediction: can the strongest ordering repair the algorithm?

The deliberately wrong executable uses an atomic count initialized to one and SeqCst loads and stores. A barrier makes both workers finish their loads before either stores zero. Predict the number of accepted reservations. Is a stronger ordering than Relaxed enough to make the pair of operations indivisible?

Prediction and its cause

Both workers report success, leaving zero available. Each operation participates in the required ordering, but the legal order is load1, load1, store0, store0. There is no data race on the atomic count. There is an application bug because two separate operations do not reserve conditionally as one transition. The barrier makes this particular bad interleaving reproducible instead of relying on unlucky timing.

Small runnable examples

Working directory: the course folder. The incorrect fixture is intentionally outside the recommended workspace. Its successful execution demonstrates a wrong result, not a recommended implementation. Put its disposable executable in the shared local output area:

mkdir -p .local/exercises
mise exec -- rustc --edition 2024 exercises/concurrency/racy_reservation.rs -o .local/exercises/racy-reservation
.local/exercises/racy-reservation
cd projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p concurrency-labs --example publication
mise exec -- cargo test -p concurrency-labs atomics

The first program prints accepted=2 remaining=0. The reference example prints a successful reservation of two units, a rejected further unit, no summary before publication and Some((3, 120)) afterward. Both use standard-library atomics. The package also contains the next lesson's Tokio example, so Cargo resolves its pinned runtime dependency even though this module does not use Tokio.

Explain the conditional transition

Budget keeps its AtomicU32 private so callers cannot increase the remaining count behind its API. checked_sub rejects requests larger than the observed count before mutation. compare_exchange_weak means: replace the count only if it still equals the value we observed. Success is the instant at which this reservation takes effect. If another worker changed the count, the operation returns the actual observed value; the loop recomputes the subtraction from that value. Weak compare-exchange may also fail spuriously, so the same loop handles a failure even without an intervening writer.

The successful compare-exchange is a useful linearization point: one instant that lets us explain a concurrent operation as though reservations happened in some sequential order. That does not make the whole program deterministic. Which worker wins is unspecified. There is no fairness or wait-free guarantee for an individual worker under arbitrary contention. Our tests use a fixed number of workers and attempts, not an unbounded producer loop.

Ordering follows the information being communicated

Relaxed preserves atomicity and the per-object modification rules but does not publish unrelated memory. It fits this single-counter budget: correctness comes from the conditional atomic update, and no reader infers anything about a separate payload from the count. It also fits the indexer's stop hint when the flag communicates only a boolean. Using Relaxed because it benchmarks faster without first defining what the flag means is not a sound rule.

The summary has a different contract. A writer stores two counts, then announces that the pair is ready. Release on the ready store and Acquire on a reader load that observes that publication establish the synchronization needed for the preceding count writes to be observed afterward. The individual count accesses remain atomic and use Relaxed; the publication flag carries the ordering relationship. Acquire is not a command to fetch the universally newest value. A load can still observe false and return None. The API promises a valid summary if it observes publication, not an arbitrary deadline for doing so.

The Publisher is not Clone and publishing consumes it. That ownership rule is essential: the counts are never overwritten after ready becomes true. Reusing a true flag for later updates would allow readers to combine different generations. Supporting repeated publication needs a different contract, such as a mutex-protected snapshot or a channel carrying owned snapshots. A memory-ordering change alone does not create that generation protocol. The reader deliberately returns None when the publisher is dropped without publishing; it does not spin forever or invent a result.

AcqRel combines acquire and release effects for a read-modify-write operation. SeqCst adds a single ordering for sequentially consistent operations, subject to Rust's documented model. Neither makes a sequence of loads and stores a multi-object transaction. Not every ordering is valid for every operation: a load cannot publish a prior write using Release, and a store cannot acquire a later observation. Read the operation's signature and documentation rather than trying orderings until compilation succeeds.

Deliberate mistake and the playbook investigation

Observation: the barrier fixture accepts two reservations. Hypothesis A says the failure comes from weak visibility and SeqCst will fix it. Hypothesis B says the gap lies between checking and changing. The fixture already uses SeqCst, so its repeated wrong result disproves A for this reproduction. Next, replace the two-step transition with Budget::try_take while keeping the same initial budget and number of callers. The relevant claim is the number accepted, not whether threads happened to run in a pleasing order.

For publication, do not claim that a Relaxed-only variant is correct because a million runs showed the expected counts. The missing observation is a allowed-but-unseen execution under the memory model. Separate the normative argument from dynamic evidence. A model checker such as Loom can explore a bounded model when a custom concurrent algorithm justifies that extra work; this lab does not claim an executed Loom proof.

Guided project checkpoint and deadlock reasoning

Read the indexer's cancellation flag and receiver lock next to this lab. Write the invariant protected by each. Retain its channel-based admission: the channel does more than count. Add a diagnostic counter only if you need that measurement, keeping the counter distinct from authoritative admission. Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p07-indexer and explain why an atomic progress count need not establish that a result has been safely stored.

A mutex is often the clearer alternative when several fields must change together. It protects a critical section; its guard releases the lock when dropped. With two locks, opposite acquisition order can deadlock: thread A holds X waiting for Y while B holds Y waiting for X. Stronger atomics elsewhere do not break that cycle. First ask whether one owner can receive commands through a channel or one small mutex can cover the invariant. If multiple locks are justified, define one acquisition order, such as ascending stable account ID, and follow it on every path. Do not hold a synchronous guard across await. A lock's scope should follow the invariant, not simply the largest convenient block.

Independent practice

Specify whether taking zero units succeeds; explain why the reference permits it. Implement a bounded return operation that cannot exceed an initial capacity, or explain why storing that second invariant makes a mutex simpler. Draw the state transitions before coding. Independently diagnose a two-lock transfer design with opposite caller argument orders; give a safe design without relying on a timing test to happen to hang. For the publication lab, explain why adding Clone to Publisher changes its correctness argument.

Hint 1

For returning units, prevent both numeric overflow and exceeding the configured capacity. Distinguish a reported progress metric from authority to admit work.

Hint 2

Try a small capacity such as two and enumerate take/return sequences. For locks, give the resources stable identities independent of the caller's source/destination order.

Reference approach

A private immutable capacity plus a compare-exchange loop can bound a single available count on return, but it cannot by itself prove that a caller legitimately owns units to return. A reservation token whose Drop returns its units can express that ownership; this introduces lifetime and cancellation choices that need review. A small mutex-protected ledger may be more appropriate. For transfers, acquiring lower-ID then higher-ID locks makes ordering consistent; reject a self-transfer or handle its single-lock case explicitly. Tests should cover invalid returns, same-resource operations and concurrent conservation, not merely final formatting.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The lab uses a private atomic budget and a one-use publication owner because those types make their narrow invariants explicit. It uses Arc only for the two genuine shared owners of publication state. The indexer keeps its higher-level channel. Native tests check reservation conservation under sixteen bounded workers, oversized requests and publication API states; the intentional fixture forces the counterexample even with SeqCst. These observations do not prove every hardware execution or fairness. Expanding to repeated snapshots, resource tokens or a wait-free algorithm would require a new design argument and stronger testing.

When you get stuck and mastery check

Write the smallest forbidden outcome first. List the memory operations that could produce it and identify the exact synchronization edge you believe rules it out. Bring a reviewer the invariant, one controlled interleaving and the relevant standard-library ordering documentation. Explain, without the reference, why a data-race-free program can still overspend a budget, why Acquire/Release is appropriate for the one-use summary, and why a mutex may be the more professional choice for a larger state transition.

title: Pinning and preserving progress across await
summary: Keep one future alive across repeated polls, and distinguish a total deadline from an idle timeout.
objectives: Explain Pin and Unpin through a timer that actually requires pinning
Distinguish a future owner from a temporary pinned reborrow
Preserve one absolute deadline while processing bounded input
Test cancellation and temporal behavior with a controlled Tokio clock
body:
Purpose: a busy input must not postpone its deadline forever

A service operation should collect messages for at most ten milliseconds of runtime time. Messages arrive every four milliseconds. If receiving a message starts a fresh ten-millisecond timer, the operation can continue indefinitely under steady input. That program implements an idle timeout rather than the promised total deadline. This lesson gives the operation one timer whose state survives each trip through the selection loop, then uses that concrete need to explain pinning.

Plain-English model: a paused computation is a value

Calling an async function creates a future: a value that represents work and its progress. An executor polls that future. Poll can return Ready with its result, or Pending after arranging for useful progress to cause a wakeup. A wakeup asks the executor to poll again; it does not promise immediate execution. State needed after await is retained in the future. Some such states can contain relationships that would become invalid if the stored value moved after polling began.

Pin is an API contract for a pointer to a value whose location must remain stable when that type requires it. It does not freeze every field, select a physical stack address in advance, or automatically make a program faster. Unpin marks types that do not need this restriction. Most ordinary types are Unpin; a particular future, such as Tokio's Sleep, may not be. Moving a pinned owning pointer is different from moving the value it points to. A Pin<Box<T>> can move its handle while retaining the allocation holding T.

The standard Future polling interface receives a pinned mutable reference. That lets an executor honor the future's contract while the future advances its internal state. This lesson does not implement raw-pointer projection or unsafe pinning. We use the runtime's documented pinning macro and the safe APIs of an existing future. Knowing when not to implement a custom Future is useful engineering judgment.

Prediction: total time versus silence between messages

At virtual time zero, collection begins with a deadline at 10. Input arrives at 4,8,12 and16. Predict the accepted items if the timer is created once at the beginning. Then predict the deadline if a fresh ten-unit sleep is created after each input. State whether these are two implementations of the same contract or two different contracts.

Prediction explained

The absolute-deadline implementation collects the first two items and stops at 10. Recreating a relative sleep after each item postpones expiration; with an open channel and no more input, it can stop at 26. That can be a valid inactivity policy when explicitly required. It is a defect when the specification promises a total operation budget. Do not call every simple timer reset unprofessional; name the requirement that makes it wrong here.

Small runnable checkpoint

Working directory: projects/. These are complete reference files in the shared native workspace. The example sends two bounded fixture values, closes the sender and prints items=[7, 8] stop=Closed. Its main returns Result so channel and collection failures have an explicit process boundary.

mise exec -- cargo run -p concurrency-labs --example deadline
mise exec -- cargo test -p concurrency-labs deadlines
mise exec -- cargo clippy -p concurrency-labs --all-targets -- -D warnings

Explain the retained future

sleep_until(deadline) creates one Sleep future outside the loop. tokio::pin!(timer) pins that local value safely. Each select call borrows it again with &mut timer; it does not create another timer or take ownership away from the operation. The selected temporary reborrow can end while the original timer and its registration remain alive. Dropping the whole operation ends the owner's lifetime and drops its timer.

Compare this with Box::pin. Boxing would create an owned pinned allocation that can be returned or stored beyond a local scope. It is unnecessary for this local operation. Pinning does not inherently require a heap allocation. Neither a browser animation nor the presence of a Box proves a type's safety obligations; the Rust types and the implementation's invariants establish what callers may do.

The collection function borrows the receiver and shutdown watcher. The caller still owns the channel endpoints. Successfully received items move into the report, while unread queued values remain in the receiver when the operation returns. Capacity is at most 1,024, validated before allocation. A zero maximum completes immediately with Limit unless shutdown was already observed. A future deadline, a closed data channel, a reached item limit and cancellation have distinct result variants. Distinguishing them makes a caller's retry or shutdown decision reviewable.

The selection uses an explicit priority. A shutdown value already observed as true stops collection. Otherwise a ready deadline is checked before ordinary watch updates or data; its branch rechecks the shutdown value. This avoids letting repeated false-valued watch updates postpone an expired deadline. Closing the shutdown sender also ends collection when that event is selected. No synchronous mutex guard crosses await. The example holds its shutdown sender until collection ends: dropping it early would be a real control message, not an irrelevant local cleanup.

Cancellation safety is about retained progress

Tokio documents receiving from its bounded mpsc receiver as cancellation safe for use in select: canceling an uncompleted receive does not remove a message from the channel. That property is specific to the operation. A composite future that has already consumed half a network frame may retain progress only inside itself. If a loop drops and recreates that future whenever another branch wins, consumed bytes do not reappear on the socket. The chat project's persistent reader future exists for that reason.

Keeping the future alive preserves its state; pinning satisfies the constraints required to poll that value in place. These are connected ideas, not synonyms. A type can be Unpin while still holding important progress that must not be thrown away. Conversely, pinning a future does not make its externally visible effects reversible. If cancellation follows a database commit, dropping the client future cannot uncommit the transaction.

Deliberate mistake: demanding an unrestricted mutable reference

The intentionally failing file exercises/concurrency/pinned_get_mut.rs creates a value containing PhantomPinned, pins it in a Box and then calls get_mut on the pinned reference. From the course folder run mise exec -- rustc --edition 2024 exercises/concurrency/pinned_get_mut.rs. Expected result: E0277 because the type does not satisfy Unpin. This fixture demonstrates a type boundary; it is not a sound self-referential container implementation.

Do not repair the error by adding unsafe pointer code you cannot justify or by declaring Unpin without understanding the type. For an ordinary value that does not require address stability, choose an ordinary mutable reference from the start. For Sleep, use its documented pinned methods, such as reset when intentionally implementing a new deadline policy. The safe reference collector needs no raw pointers.

Playbook investigation: the deadline keeps moving

Observation: a monitor under steady input does not stop at the promised total budget. Hypothesis A says runtime scheduling is occasionally late. Hypothesis B says the program recreates a relative timer whenever another branch completes. Instrument creation and expiry instants with synthetic timestamps; reduce to one receiver and four planned messages. Under Tokio's paused test clock, the reference stops exactly at virtual10 with two items. A recreated relative timer has a different expected timeline. That controlled experiment weakens scheduling delay as the explanation for this minimal reproduction.

The tests enable Tokio's test-util feature only for development. Paused time controls Tokio's clock in the test runtime; it does not virtualize arbitrary OS threads, blocking filesystem calls or remote servers. An exact virtual-time assertion checks our timer ownership and selection logic, not a promise about ten-millisecond wall-clock latency on a loaded machine. The producer task is explicitly aborted and awaited after the deadline test, so it cannot silently keep running in the background.

Guided project increment

Trace the health monitor's endpoint deadline from argument validation to each retry attempt. Write which instant bounds the whole operation and which duration bounds one attempt. In a learner copy, extract a small bounded receiver collection step using this reference's signature. Begin with the closed-channel example; then add the already-cancelled case and the steady-arrival timeline before connecting real network I/O. Use a separately retained timer or a fixed absolute instant whenever the budget belongs to the entire operation.

Do not introduce spawning merely to call select. Its branches are polled concurrently on the current task; they do not automatically execute on different OS threads. Blocking CPU work inside a branch can prevent the timer from being polled at all. Move genuinely blocking work to an appropriate bounded worker design and explain what cancellation can interrupt. A deadline future is cooperative scheduling, not an operating-system kill switch.

Independent practice and tiered hints

Implement an explicitly named idle-timeout variant, and test how its timeline differs. Specify the result when cancellation, channel closure, a full item limit and deadline all become observable together. Add a test proving that unread values remain available after Limit. Finally, explain how a partially decoded frame could be lost even though each individual socket read is memory safe.

Hint 1

Write an event timeline before editing. Decide whether a successfully received item is supposed to extend the allowed time.

Hint 2

For idle time, retain one pinned Sleep and reset it through its documented pinned API after accepting a message. Keep a separate absolute deadline if both limits are required.

Reference approach

An idle variant can reset its timer to now plus the idle interval after each accepted value. Its contract must name that extension. A combined policy keeps a fixed total deadline and uses the earlier of that instant and the current idle deadline. Tests need a steady stream, a long silent interval and simultaneous stop conditions. For framed I/O, retain the parser future or move partially consumed bytes into a persistent decoder buffer rather than discarding them whenever another branch wins.

Engineering decisions, evidence and mastery

The implementation uses a borrowed bounded receiver, one locally pinned timer, a bounded output vector and an explicit stop enum. Pinning is justified by an actual !Unpin timer; heap pinning and unsafe projection are omitted because they add no capability this operation needs. Seven laboratory tests cover atomic and temporal contracts, including the controlled deadline, unread items and cancellation distinctions. The intentional compiler fixture separately confirms the expected trait restriction. These checks do not establish browser timing, remote service behavior or every scheduler interleaving.

When you get stuck, identify which value owns the progress and which value is dropped when a branch loses. Share the smallest timer/channel program, predicted timeline, observed stop reason and pinned API documentation. You are ready to move on when you can explain why the timer survives each selection, change the deadline policy without accidental resets, and debug a lost-progress example without treating Pin as a magic performance annotation.
